title: Assignment 3
text:
Data and variables
This assignment uses the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates to examine income and poverty across New York City census tracts. The study area includes Bronx, Kings (Brooklyn), New York (Manhattan), Queens, and Richmond (Staten Island) counties. Census tracts make it possible to explore variation within the city rather than relying on a single citywide average.
The data come from S0701, Geographic Mobility by Selected Characteristics in the United States. Although its main topic is mobility, its total-population column also includes income and poverty estimates. The income measure is median individual income among people aged 15 and older, expressed in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars. It is not median household income. The poverty measure covers people aged one and older for whom poverty status is determined.








Variable ID
Variable name
Measure




S0701_C01_048
income
Median individual income, age 15+


S0701_C01_050
pov
People age 1+ below 100% of the poverty level


S0701_C01_049
povden
People age 1+ for whom poverty status is determined





Analysis

library(tigris)

             pov = "S0701_C01_050", # people below 100 percent of the poverty level

  geography = geo_level,

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS


Using the ACS Subject Tables

acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
  mutate(pov_rate = povE / povdenE,
         pov_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM))


Poverty rates
A poverty count depends on the number of residents, so I divide it by the relevant population denominator:
\[
\text{Poverty rate}=\frac{\text{People below the poverty level}}{\text{People for whom poverty status is determined}}.
\]

ggplot(acs_wide) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Median Individual Income (age 15+)", na.value = "snow2") +
  labs(title = paste0("ACS ", year_acs, " 5-year: Median Individual Income — ",
                      state_abbr, " (", geo_level, ")"),
       caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau via tidycensus") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.03, 0.97),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1))








The map shows variation in median individual income across New York City census tracts. Several higher-income tracts appear in Manhattan, while many tracts elsewhere have lower estimated incomes. White areas represent missing income estimates, rather than zero income.

Uncertainty check
For Queens County Census Tract 179.02, the approximate 90% confidence interval is 100% ± 77.14 percentage points, or [22.86%, 177.14%]. For Bronx County Census Tract 319, it is 88% ± 19.76 percentage points, or [68.24%, 107.76%]. Although percentages cannot exceed 100%, these unbounded intervals illustrate the large uncertainty associated with the estimates. Restricting the endpoints to the feasible 0–100% range gives [22.86%, 100%] and [68.24%, 100%]. The intervals overlap substantially. Therefore, the ranking reflects the order of point estimates and does not establish that Queens Tract 179.02 has a higher underlying poverty rate than Bronx Tract 319. Overlap alone is not a formal test of the difference.


Methods note
I retrieved 2020–2024 ACS 5-year estimates using tidycensus for census tracts in New York City’s five counties. I selected three variables from Subject Table S0701: median individual income for residents aged 15 and older, the number of residents below the poverty level, and the corresponding poverty-status population denominator. I mapped income and calculated poverty rates to compare areas with different population sizes. I retained the margins of error and used moe_prop() to propagate uncertainty into the poverty proportions. The tables present the ten highest and lowest estimated poverty rates alongside their MOEs. Rates and MOEs in the R output are proportions; multiplying them by 100 gives percentages and percentage-point MOEs. Overlapping approximate 90% confidence intervals limit confidence in the rankings. Small populations and large MOEs require particular caution. These estimates summarize a five-year period rather than conditions in 2024 alone.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Query Parameters

Search terms: Trump, Harris, and Election
Geography: Worldwide
Time window: Past 5 years
Category: Crime & Justice
Search type: Web Search
Retrieval date and time: September 15, 2026, 1:39 PM

I first collected Google Trends data manually from the website and then reproduced the query using the gtrendsR package in R. The five-year window produced weekly observations. When I changed the time window to the past 30 days, the observations changed to daily intervals.
Google Trends values are normalized relative search-interest scores rather than raw search counts or percentages. A value of 100 represents the peak search interest within the selected query, while 0 indicates very low relative search interest rather than necessarily zero searches.

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr) 

TrumpHarrisElection = gtrends(c("Trump","Harris","election"), onlyInterest = TRUE, gprop = "web", time = "today+5-y", category = 704, ) # last five years
the_df=TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)

Warning: `aes_string()` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.0.0.
ℹ Please use tidy evaluation idioms with `aes()`.
ℹ See also `vignette("ggplot2-in-packages")` for more information.
ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the gtrendsR package.
  Please report the issue at <https://github.com/PMassicotte/gtrendsR/issues>.








write_csv(the_df, paste0("gtrends_worldwide_5y_CrimeJustice", Sys.Date(), ".csv")) 



Search Term and Measurement Changes
When I removed Election and repeated the search using only Trump and Harris, the values for the remaining terms remained similar. Because Election had relatively low search interest in the original query, its removal produced only minor changes in the normalized values.

TrumpHarris <- gtrends(c("Trump", "Harris"), onlyInterest = TRUE,  gprop = "web", time = "today+5-y", category = 704, )

TrumpHarris_df <- TrumpHarris$interest_over_time 
plot(TrumpHarris) 









TrumpKamalaHarris <- gtrends(c("Trump", "Kamala Harris"), onlyInterest = TRUE,  gprop = "web", time = "today+5-y", category = 704, )

TrumpKamalaHarris_df <- TrumpKamalaHarris$interest_over_time 
plot(TrumpKamalaHarris) 








I also compared “Kamala Harris” with “Harris.” The two series were different. This matters because a search term does not necessarily measure the exact concept of interest. “Harris” can refer to people, places, or organizations other than Kamala Harris, while “Kamala Harris” is a more specific search term.


Website versus R code
The website and R results were identical when I used the same search terms. The values and overall temporal patterns matched across the two methods.
The two approaches differ methodologically. Manual website downloads require the researcher to record the search settings separately, while R code directly documents many of the query parameters and therefore provides clearer provenance. R is also more scalable because many terms or locations can be collected programmatically rather than downloaded individually. However, R code can be fragile because it relies on the Google Trends service rather than an official public API. Reproducibility is also imperfect because Google Trends relies on sampled and normalized search data.
When I repeated the same R query a few minutes later, the results were slightly different. This suggests that findings based on Google Trends should be interpreted as relative and potentially sample-dependent measures rather than fixed counts.

title: Assignment 4
text:
Alternative Wikipedia Table: NHL Teams
I applied the same web scraping approach to the “List of teams” table on Wikipedia’s National Hockey League page. The table contained 32 teams and 11 variables, including conference, division, team, city, arena, capacity, founding year, and other organizational characteristics.
Unlike the foreign exchange reserves table, the NHL table did not require removing repeated header rows. However, the cleaning code needed to be modified because the column names and variable formats differed. I changed the column names and converted arena capacity, founding year, and joining year into numeric variables.
After cleaning, the dataset contained 32 observations with no missing values or duplicate teams. All four divisions contained eight teams each. This demonstrates that even when the same html_table() function works across webpages, the data cleaning process must be adjusted to accommodate differences in table structure.

title: Assignment 4
section: Comparison of Wikipedia and World Bank Data
text:
Comparison of Wikipedia and World Bank Data
The Wikipedia and World Bank datasets report the same general concept of total foreign exchange reserves. However, they differ in their reporting periods, country naming conventions, and data collection methods.
The Wikipedia table includes observations from different reporting dates, while the World Bank comparison uses annual observations from 2024. Therefore, differences between the reported values may reflect changes over time rather than accuracy problems between the two sources.
In addition, some countries could not initially be matched because the two datasets used different country names. Country names were standardized where possible to improve comparability.

title: Assignment 4
text:
When Is Web Scraping Appropriate?
Web scraping is appropriate when the required data are publicly accessible on a webpage but are not available through an API or another structured, machine-readable source. However, when an official API is available, it is generally preferable because it offers a more consistent and reproducible method of data collection.

title: Assignment 4
text:
Data Source
This study will examines the spatial relationship between correctional facility proximity and county-level crime rates in Texas. Facility information will be collected from the official Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) Unit Directory. The directory provides facility names, administrative regions, facility types, cities, and counties, while individual facility pages provide more detailed information, including physical addresses and operational characteristics. This official source is preferred over third-party databases because it provides information directly maintained by the responsible state agency.

title: Assignment 4
text:
Robots.txt and Terms of Service
Before scraping, the website’s robots.txt file will be checked using the robotstxt package in R. The current file does not list the Unit Directory among its disallowed paths. The website’s applicable terms and policies will also be reviewed to ensure compliance with restrictions on automated access and reuse of information. Data collection will be limited to publicly accessible facility information, with attribution to TDCJ and the retrieval date documented.

title: Assignment 4
text:
API Availability and Scraping Justification
No publicly documented API providing the required facility-level information was identified for the TDCJ Unit Directory. Although the website provides structured listings of correctional facilities, detailed information is distributed across individual webpages. Therefore, web scraping using the rvest package is appropriate for collecting and consolidating facility information into a single dataset. If a suitable official API or downloadable dataset becomes available, it will be preferred over scraping.

title: Assignment 4
section: Data Volume, Rate Limiting, and Caching
text:
Data Volume, Rate Limiting, and Caching
The collection will focus on correctional facilities in TDCJ Region II, with potential expansion to other regions for broader geographic comparisons. The scraper will first collect facility names and links from the Unit Directory, then visit individual facility pages to extract addresses and relevant characteristics. Requests will be sent sequentially with a delay of approximately one to two seconds between requests to minimize server load. Retrieved information will be stored locally as CSV files, including the source URL and collection date, to avoid repeated requests during data cleaning and analysis.

title: Assignment 4
text:
Website Changes and Data Validation
Changes in HTML structure, element names, or page layouts may cause the scraper to miss or incorrectly extract information. In particular, extraction methods relying on fixed XPath expressions may fail when webpage structures change. To identify these problems, the collected dataset will be checked for missing addresses, duplicate facilities, unexpected changes in record counts, and inconsistent variable formats. Selected records will also be manually compared with the original TDCJ webpages. These procedures will improve the transparency and reproducibility of the data collection process.
